intro: This unit is about how the Talmud is studied, and what it teaches about being kind. You will see two people share one page. They read out loud. They ask questions. They disagree, and they stay friends.

Then you will read seven kindness rules the rabbis wrote down. Visiting the sick. Welcoming a guest. Honoring parents. Not shaming anyone. Bringing back lost things. Giving a share. Feeding animals first.
By the end, you will be able to study with a partner the way the rabbis did. And you will be able to say who each kindness rule helps.
bigQuestion: How do people learn the Talmud together, and who do its kindness rules help?

timeline.t: Find a partner. In Jewish tradition, a study partner is called a chavruta.
Open one page between you. Sit close. Both of you look at the same line.
Read a line out loud. Then let your partner read the next one.
Stuck on a word? Ask. Hillel said a shy person cannot learn.
Disagree? Say why, and say it gently. Point to the page.
Remember the two houses. They argued for years and still stayed one family.
Read a kindness rule from the rabbis, like visiting the sick.
Say who the rule helps. The guest, the parent, the owner, the animal.
Try one rule this week. Then tell your partner how it went.

words.d: a study partner; two people who read the Talmud together and ask each other questions
a house of study, a room where people learn Talmud, often in pairs and out loud
a short book of rabbis' sayings inside the Mishnah; the name means chapters of the fathers
the students who followed Hillel's way of reading the rules
a rule in the Torah; the rabbis also use it for a good deed; more than one is mitzvot
to make someone feel small in front of others; the rabbis said never to do it
a secret detail that shows a lost thing is really yours
giving a share to people who need it; the word comes from a word for fair

test.why: A chavruta is a study partner. The word comes from a word for friend.

test.q: How did the rabbis study the Talmud?
choices: Out loud, in pairs, with questions
test.why: Jewish tradition studies the Talmud out loud with a partner, asking questions.

test.q: Who said to get yourself a teacher and a friend?
test.why: The saying is Joshua ben Perachyah's, in Pirkei Avot 1:6.

test.q: What did the Talmud's voice call both houses' words?
test.why: Eruvin 13b says these and those are the words of the living God.

test.q: Why does the Talmud say the rule follows Hillel's house?
choices: They were gentle and taught the other side first
test.why: The Talmud says Hillel's students were gentle and taught Shammai's view before their own.
A mitzvah is a rule in the Torah. The rabbis also use it for a good deed.

test.q: Who ran to welcome three strangers?
test.why: Genesis 18 says Abraham ran to the strangers and fed them.

test.q: What does the owner of a lost thing give the finder?
test.why: The Mishnah in Bava Metzia says the owner gives a sign, a secret detail.

choices: Giving a share to people in need
test.why: Tzedakah is giving a share to people who need it. The word comes from a word for fair.

test.q: When does the Talmud say to feed your animals?
test.why: Berakhot 40a says to feed your animals before you sit down to eat.

write.prompt: Pick one kindness rule from this unit. Tell what the Torah or the Talmud says about it. Name where it comes from, like Genesis 18 or Bava Metzia. Then say who the rule helps and how you could do it.
tips: Name the book or tractate you are talking about.
Say "the rabbis said" or "the Torah says" when you tell what it teaches.
Use a word from this unit, like mitzvah or chavruta.
Tell who the rule helps, and one thing you could do.
